title: Germany Is Officially Adrift
gist: After a CDU 'disaster' in September state elections (below 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, AfD first with 38% there and ~44% in Saxony-Anhalt, Left first in Berlin), Chancellor Merz survives only because rivals don't want to own painful reforms. Rathke argues Germany's party system has lost alternation, the east is becoming a de facto AfD-vs-one-mainstream two-party system, and Merz's shrinking bandwidth will weaken German leadership on European defense and Ukraine ahead of 2027 western state elections covering ~37% of voters.

insights.claim: The CDU fell below the 5 percent threshold in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the first time in postwar history it failed to win state-level representation, while the AfD won first place with 38 percent there and nearly 44 percent in Saxony-Anhalt.
insights.speaker: Jeff Rathke
insights.so_what: Signals structural erosion of Germany's governing party and rising far-right strength, a European political-risk factor.
insights.quote: The CDU fell below the 5 percent threshold in the east German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern—the first time in postwar German history that the CDU has failed to win representation in a state election.

insights.claim: 84 percent of Germans say they are unhappy with the performance of Merz's government.
insights.speaker: Jeff Rathke
insights.so_what: Deep unpopularity limits the government's capacity to pass reforms.

insights.claim: The severity of Germany's situation is Merz's short-term insurance policy: rivals avoid toppling him because they would have to own the bitter reform medicine.

insights.so_what: Leadership change is less likely near-term than polls imply, but at the cost of weakened authority.
